passages.t: A plot, a jar of perfume, and a betrayal
passages.happening: It is two days before the Passover. The chief priests and scribes want to arrest Jesus quietly and kill him, but not during the feast, in case the people riot. Meanwhile, in the village of Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the home of a man called Simon the Leper. A woman comes in with an alabaster jar of very costly perfume made of pure nard. She breaks the jar and pours the perfume on Jesus' head. Some at the table are angry. It could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor. Jesus defends her. She has done a beautiful thing, he says. She has anointed his body ahead of time for burial, and wherever the good news is preached, her story will be told. Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, goes to the chief priests and offers to hand Jesus over. They are glad and promise him money.
passages.hearers:
Passover was the great feast that remembered how God brought Israel out of slavery in Egypt. Pilgrims crowded into Jerusalem for it. A feast about freedom, under Roman rule, in a packed city, could turn dangerous fast. Josephus tells of a Passover around AD 48 to 50 when Roman soldiers were posted above the temple courts, a soldier insulted the crowd, a riot broke out, and thousands died in the crush (Jewish War 2.224-227). The leaders' fear of a riot was not imaginary.

Nard was a perfume made from a plant that grows in the Himalayan mountains. It came a long way and cost a great deal. A denarius was a day's pay for a laborer (Matthew 20:2), so three hundred denarii was close to a year's wages. An alabaster jar was a small stone flask. Breaking its neck meant pouring out all of it at once. There was no saving some for later.

Pouring oil on someone's head was a sign of honor. It was also how Israel's kings were anointed. The woman does for Jesus what a prophet once did for a king. Jesus gives it another meaning too: bodies were anointed for burial.
passages.ot:
When Jesus says “The poor you will always have with you,” he is echoing the law of Moses: “For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land” (Deuteronomy 15:11). The verse in Deuteronomy is a command to be generous. Jesus is not excusing anyone from caring for the poor. He even adds that they can help the poor whenever they want.

The psalm says of God the host, “You anoint my head with oil” (Psalm 23:5).
passages.hard: Why does Judas do it? Mark does not say. He mentions money, but only as something the priests promise after Judas comes to them. Matthew speaks of thirty pieces of silver, and John says Judas stole from the common purse. Readers have guessed at disappointment, greed, or a plan to force Jesus' hand. Mark leaves the motive dark and puts the story of Judas right next to the story of the woman. One gives away something precious for Jesus. The other gives Jesus away for money.
passages.asks: The woman did not count the cost, and the people around her did. Jesus called her gift beautiful. Ask whether there is something you are holding back from Jesus because it seems too costly or too much. Notice, too, that people who say ‘think of the poor’ are not always thinking of the poor. Jesus cared for both: the woman's love and the poor.

passages.t: The Passover room and the betrayer at the table
passages.happening: On the day the Passover lambs are sacrificed, the disciples ask where they should get the meal ready. Jesus sends two of them into the city. A man carrying a jar of water will meet them. They are to follow him and ask the owner of the house for the guest room. They find a large upstairs room, ready, just as Jesus said. That evening, while they are eating, Jesus says that one of them will betray him. They are upset and ask one by one, “Surely not I?” He says it is one of the Twelve, someone dipping bread into the bowl with him.
passages.hearers:
The Passover lambs were killed at the temple in the afternoon and eaten that night inside the city. Families from out of town needed a room, and people in Jerusalem made rooms available to pilgrims.

Carrying water was usually women's work. A man with a water jar would stand out in a crowded street. Jesus may have arranged this in advance as a quiet signal. With the priests looking for a way to arrest him, the place of the meal was kept secret even from the Twelve.

Sharing bread from one bowl was a sign of friendship. To betray someone you had eaten with was a deep shame in that world, as in ours.
passages.ot:
The words ‘one who is eating with Me’ echo a psalm of David about a friend who turned against him: “Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me” (Psalm 41:9).

The Passover itself goes back to Exodus 12. God told Israel to keep it every year, and that when children ask what it means, the parents must tell the story.
passages.hard:
Jesus says “The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed!” If God's plan included the betrayal, was Judas still to blame? Mark holds both together without explaining how. God's purpose stands, and Judas is responsible for what he chose. Christians from different traditions explain that tension in different ways, but none of them says Judas was a puppet. Notice also that each disciple asks ‘Surely not I?’ None of them points at someone else. Each one wonders about himself.

There is also a question of dates. Mark presents this meal as the Passover meal itself (verse 12). John's Gospel seems to place it a day earlier. In John, on the morning of the trial the priests had not yet eaten the Passover (John 18:28), and Jesus is sentenced on “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14), so he dies while the lambs are being killed. Christians have answered in several ways. Some argue that John's words refer to other meals and the Friday of the feast week, so that John and Mark agree. Some suggest that different groups kept different calendars, so that Jesus ate the Passover earlier than the temple did; the French scholar Annie Jaubert argued for this, and critics doubt such a calendar was in use. Some think Jesus held a farewell meal full of Passover meaning on the evening before the official Passover. And some think one Gospel arranged the timing to make a point, John to show Jesus as the Passover lamb. No answer has won general agreement. All four Gospels agree that Jesus died at Passover time, on a Friday, and that his death is to be understood in the light of the exodus.
passages.asks: Every disciple at that table thought, at least for a moment, that it might be him. That is a healthy fear. Ask yourself the same question when you read of Judas and Peter: not ‘how could they?’ but ‘could I?’ Jesus still shared the bowl with the man who would betray him. He did not throw him out.

passages.t: This is My body; this is My blood
passages.happening: During the meal Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to the disciples. “Take it; this is My body.” Then he takes a cup, gives thanks, and they all drink from it. “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” He tells them that he will not drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. They sing a hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives.
passages.hearers:
A Passover meal was a meal with words. The head of the table explained what the food meant: the bread made in a hurry, the bitter herbs, the lamb. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, describes the meal in its later form: everyone, even the poorest, reclines at the table as free people do, and there are four cups of wine and songs from the Psalms (Mishnah Pesachim 10). How much of that order was already fixed in Jesus' day is debated. But the pattern of a host explaining the food fits exactly what Jesus does.

What would have shocked the disciples is what he says the food means. He does not explain the bread by the exodus. He says it is his body. He does not explain the cup by Egypt. He says it is his blood, poured out for many.

The hymn was most likely from the Psalms of praise sung at Passover, Psalms 113 to 118, which end, “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good.”
passages.ot:
At Mount Sinai Moses sealed God's covenant with Israel with blood and said, “This is the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). A covenant is a binding promise between God and his people. Jesus uses the same words for his own blood.

Jeremiah had promised, “I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah” (Jeremiah 31:31).

And Isaiah's suffering servant “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:12). Jesus' ‘poured out for many’ echoes that line.
passages.hard: What does ‘This is My body’ mean? Christians have read these words in different ways, and the disagreement is old and serious. The Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed churches teach that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and that believers feed on him by faith. Many Baptist and other churches see the meal mainly as a memorial, a way of remembering his death as he commanded (1 Corinthians 11:24). These notes do not settle the question. Every one of these churches agrees that Jesus gave this meal to his followers, that it points to his death for them, and that it looks ahead to the kingdom.
passages.asks: Jesus gave his friends a meal on the night one of them betrayed him and the rest deserted him. He gave it to people who would fail him within hours. Ask whether you think you have to be good enough to come to his table. And ask what it means that his last promise that night was about a future meal in the kingdom of God.

passages.happening: On the way to the Mount of Olives Jesus tells the disciples that all of them will fall away. Scripture says, “I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” But after he is raised, he will go ahead of them into Galilee. Peter insists that even if everyone else falls away, he will not. Jesus tells him that this very night, before the rooster crows twice, Peter will deny him three times. Peter says he would die first, and all the others say the same.
passages.hearers:
To ‘fall away’ is to stumble and stop following. Peter's promise sounded brave and loyal. In that culture, a disciple's loyalty to his teacher was a matter of honor. To abandon your teacher in danger was shameful.

Notice what Jesus puts inside the bad news. Before Peter has even made his boast, Jesus has already promised to meet them again in Galilee. The failure is not the end of the story. The meeting place is already set.
passages.ot: The words come from the prophet Zechariah: “Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zechariah 13:7). In Zechariah it is the LORD who calls the sword against his shepherd. Jesus reads his death as part of God's purpose, and the scattering of the disciples as foretold.
passages.hard: Was Peter lying when he said he would die for Jesus? Almost certainly not. He meant it. That is the hard truth of the passage: a person can mean a promise with all their heart and still break it a few hours later. Sincerity is not the same as strength.
passages.asks: Peter trusted his own loyalty. Jesus did not. But Jesus also did not give up on Peter. Ask where you are most sure of yourself, and whether that confidence rests on you or on him. And notice that the promise of Galilee was spoken before the failure. Grace was waiting before Peter needed it.

passages.happening: They come to a place called Gethsemane. Jesus takes Peter, James, and John further in and begins to be deeply troubled and distressed. He says, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death. Stay here and keep watch.” He goes a little farther, falls to the ground, and prays that if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. “Abba, Father,” he prays, “all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.” Three times he comes back and finds his friends asleep. “The spirit is willing,” he says, “but the body is weak.” The third time he tells them the hour has come. His betrayer is near.
passages.hearers:
Gethsemane is usually explained as meaning ‘oil press’. It seems to have been an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives, across the valley from the temple. The exact spot is not known.

Abba is the Aramaic word for father. Children used it, and so did grown children. To pray to God with this family word was unusual, and Mark keeps the Aramaic so his readers can hear Jesus' own voice.

A ‘cup’ in the prophets could stand for the suffering God's judgment brings. Isaiah speaks of Jerusalem drinking “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17). Many Christians have read Jesus' cup this way: not only death, but the weight of sin and judgment he was about to carry for others.

Remember the end of chapter 13. Jesus told the disciples to keep watch, because the master might come in the night and find them sleeping. Here it happens, three times.
passages.ot:
Jesus' words of sorrow echo a lament in the Psalms: “Why are you downcast, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5). The psalm-writer pours out his grief to God and still calls him “my God.” Jesus does the same.

The letter to the Hebrews remembers this kind of prayer: “He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death” (Hebrews 5:7).
passages.hard:
Why would the Son of God dread death and ask to be spared? Critics of Christianity have asked this since the early centuries. A god, they said, would not tremble. The church's answer has been that Jesus was truly human, with a real human soul and a real human will. He felt horror at death and at the cup, as a real man would. And he freely gave his will to the Father's. The scene shows not that he was less than God, but that he truly became one of us.

This passage also speaks to anyone who has known sorrow so heavy it felt like dying. Jesus did not hide that sorrow. He said it out loud, to his friends and to his Father. If you are in a place like that, you are not wrong to say so, and you should not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live.
passages.asks: Jesus' prayer has two halves, and both are honest. ‘Take this cup from Me’ is a real request. ‘Yet not what I will, but what You will’ is a real surrender. Ask whether you allow yourself to pray the first half, and whether you can pray the second. Notice also how gently Jesus speaks to his sleeping friends. He names their weakness, and he does not stop loving them.

passages.happening: While Jesus is still speaking, Judas arrives with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests, scribes, and elders. Judas has given them a signal: the one he kisses is the man. He comes straight to Jesus, says “Rabbi!” and kisses him. They seize Jesus. Someone draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Jesus asks why they have come with weapons as if he were an outlaw, when he taught openly in the temple every day. Then all the disciples run away. A young man who had been following, wearing only a linen cloth, is grabbed. He slips out of the cloth and runs off naked.
passages.hearers:
A student often greeted his teacher with a kiss. That is what made Judas's signal work. In the dark, among the olive trees, it looked like respect. It was a betrayal dressed as love.

The swords and clubs suggest the temple police and servants of the high priest, not Roman soldiers. Arresting Jesus at night, away from the crowds, was exactly what the leaders had planned at the start of the chapter.

Mark keeps a sharp detail. Peter had said he would die with Jesus. Now ‘everyone deserted Him and fled.’ Jesus is left alone.
passages.ot:
Jesus says, “this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” He has already pointed to Zechariah's shepherd struck and sheep scattered (verse 27). Here it comes true.

The prophet Amos once said that on the day of God's judgment “Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked” (Amos 2:16). Some readers hear that line behind the young man who ran away.
passages.hard: Who was the young man who fled naked? Only Mark tells this story, and he does not say. Readers have offered several answers. An old suggestion is that it was Mark himself, quietly putting himself in the scene. Others think it was simply a real person the first readers knew of. Others read it as a picture: even the last follower runs, leaving everything behind, as the disciples left everything to follow Jesus at the start (1:18). Some notice that the same word for ‘linen cloth’ is used for the cloth Jesus is buried in (15:46), and that Mark uses the same word, ‘young man’, for the figure in white at the empty tomb (16:5). None of these can be proved. It is wise not to build much on it.
passages.asks: Jesus refuses the sword. Luke adds that he healed the servant's ear (Luke 22:51). He goes with the men who came for him. Ask whether, when you are wronged, your first move is the sword or the trust Jesus shows here. And notice that Mark does not hide the disciples' running away. The first followers told the story of their own failure. The church has been honest about its failures from the start.

passages.happening: They take Jesus to the high priest, and the chief priests, elders, and scribes gather. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard and warms himself by the fire. Inside, the council looks for evidence to put Jesus to death but cannot find any. Many give false testimony, but their stories do not agree. Some claim he said he would destroy the temple and build another in three days. Jesus says nothing. At last the high priest asks him directly, “Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?” Jesus answers, “I am,” and “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” The high priest tears his clothes and calls it blasphemy. They all condemn him as deserving death. Some spit on him, blindfold him, hit him, and say, “Prophesy!”
passages.hearers:
Mark does not name the high priest. Other Gospels call him Caiaphas. In 1990, near Jerusalem, builders found a family tomb with a burial box for bones inscribed ‘Joseph son of Caiaphas’. Many scholars think it was the high priest's family tomb, though some question the identification.

The Sanhedrin was the leading council in Jerusalem, made up of chief priests, elders, and scribes, with the high priest at its head.

‘The Blessed One’ was a respectful way of saying ‘God’ without using his name.

Tearing your clothes was a sign of grief or horror. Blasphemy means speaking against God or claiming for yourself what belongs only to God.

Notice the cruel irony at the end. They mock Jesus, “Prophesy!” At that very moment, outside in the courtyard, his prophecy about Peter is coming true.
passages.ot:
Jesus' answer joins two Old Testament passages. Psalm 110:1, where the LORD says to David's Lord, “Sit at My right hand.” And Daniel 7:13, where “One like the Son of Man” comes “with the clouds of heaven” to receive a kingdom from God. He is claiming to share God's throne.

His silence before false witnesses recalls Isaiah's servant: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).
passages.hard:
Was this a lawful trial? The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, gives rules for a court in a capital case. The trial must be held by day. A guilty verdict must wait until the next day, so such a case is not heard on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1). By those rules, a night hearing at Passover breaks the law.

But scholars disagree on what that shows. Some think the Mishnah's rules, or something like them, were already in force, so the hearing was unlawful. Others point out that the Mishnah was written down long after the temple fell, and that it may describe the ideal law of later teachers rather than how the high priest's council actually worked in the 30s. On that view, it cannot be used to judge this hearing with certainty. Mark himself does not argue the legal point. He simply shows that the verdict was decided before the hearing began (14:1), and that the witnesses did not agree.

It matters to read this scene carefully. Mark names particular people: the high priest, the chief priests, elders, and scribes of that council. He does not blame the Jewish people, and Jesus, his disciples, and the crowds who loved him were all Jews.
passages.asks: Jesus stays silent when lied about, and speaks plainly when asked who he is. He does not defend himself, but he does not deny the truth to save his life. Ask whether you are more likely to defend your reputation or to tell the truth about Jesus when it costs you. Peter, at that same moment, was choosing the first.

passages.happening: Down in the courtyard a servant girl of the high priest sees Peter warming himself and says, “You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.” Peter denies it and moves out to the gateway. The rooster crows. The servant girl sees him again and tells the others he is one of them. He denies it again. A little later those standing near say, “Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.” Peter begins to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!” At once the rooster crows a second time. Peter remembers Jesus' words, and he breaks down and weeps.
passages.hearers:
A servant girl had little standing in that world. Peter, who had promised to face death, is undone by the question of a girl with no power over him at all.

People from Galilee spoke with an accent people in Jerusalem could hear. Matthew says that Peter's way of speaking gave him away (Matthew 26:73).

Peter's curse in verse 71 may mean he called down a curse on himself if he was lying. Some readers think he cursed Jesus. The Greek does not say whom he cursed.

Mark tells this story in full, with no attempt to make Peter look better. The early church told it about its own leader. Many think the story came from Peter himself.
passages.ot: The scene fulfills Jesus' own words in verse 30 and the scattering of Zechariah 13:7. There is also a contrast with Jesus inside. Jesus, under oath before the high priest, tells the truth and is condemned. Peter, before a servant girl, lies and goes free.
passages.hard:
Why does Mark record the rooster crowing twice, when the other Gospels mention one crowing? Some manuscripts of Mark also have only one, which shows that copyists noticed the difference. Most editors think Mark wrote of two crowings and some scribes made his text match the other Gospels. It does not change the story: Peter denied Jesus three times that night, just as Jesus said.

The harder question is whether Peter's failure was the end of him. Mark answers it in chapter 16, where the young man at the tomb says, “tell His disciples and Peter” (16:7). Peter is named. He has not been dropped.
passages.asks: Peter wept. That is the difference between Peter and Judas in Mark's story: one is brought back. Ask whether there is a failure you have stopped believing God could forgive. The rooster was a sound of shame for Peter. It also proved that Jesus had known all along and had chosen him anyway.
